title: Ads and tracking infiltrated TVs. Now they're coming for monitors.
gist: Computer monitors are following smart TVs into ad-serving and tracking: LG shipped an app via Windows Update driver channels that pushed McAfee ads onto connected PCs until Microsoft forced their removal, and LG and Samsung smart monitors run the same ad-serving operating systems as their TVs, positioning them for automatic content recognition. The author's warning is that ad subsidies could eventually drive monitor prices down the way they did TVs, making 'dumb' monitors as rare as dumb TVs.

insights.claim: Since at least 2024, some LG monitors installed an app called LG Monitor App Installer onto connected computers under the cover of driver updates delivered through Windows Update, and that app pushed McAfee pop-up ads onto those PCs.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The OS driver-update channel is now an ad-delivery vector — a trust breach that invites platform-level restrictions on OEM driver payloads.
insights.locator: LG lost some trust after a recent report

insights.claim: Microsoft has since forced LG to remove the McAfee ads, but the clandestine manner in which LG monitors installed ad-pushing software onto third-party devices remains the deeper concern.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Microsoft acting as enforcer establishes that OS gatekeepers, not regulators, are the practical check on peripheral-maker adware.
insights.quote: Microsoft has since forced LG to remove the McAfee ads.

insights.claim: LG Monitor App Installer's Microsoft Store listing states the app can 'use all system resources' and 'access your Internet connection,' while the brief privacy policy it links claims the app and distributed monitor applications do not collect, use, store, or share personal information.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Broad declared permissions paired with a narrow no-collection promise is a posture that can change with a single policy update — the disclosure gives no durable guarantee.
insights.quote: and the monitor applications distributed through it do not collect, use, store, or share personal information
insights.locator: LG Monitor App Installer’s page on the Microsoft Store

insights.claim: The author remains skeptical because LG has already proven it can leverage already-purchased monitors to deliver ads, meaning the capability exists regardless of current policy language.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Post-sale monetization capability, once installed, is the asset — treat privacy policies as revocable rather than protective.
insights.quote: I’m still concerned that LG could eventually leverage already-purchased monitors for more ads, as it already has proven it can, and to track user activity

insights.claim: LG's and Samsung's smart monitors run the same ad-serving operating systems as their respective smart TVs, which positions them to use automatic content recognition.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Reusing the TV OS means the ad-tech stack ships by default — monitor monetization requires no new investment, only a decision to switch it on.
insights.locator: LG’s and Samsung’s smart monitors use the same

insights.claim: Users of LG and Samsung smart monitors, including the reviews site RTINGs, have already shown the displays tracking user activity, though neither company had responded on whether their smart monitors use ACR.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Third-party testers, not vendors, are the source of truth on display tracking — vendor silence on ACR is itself informative.
insights.locator: Users of LG and Samsung smart monitors

insights.claim: The privacy policies for monitors from LG, Samsung, and Acer all state that the companies may share data collected from their devices with advertisers.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Advertiser data-sharing is already permitted across all three named vendors' policies — the legal groundwork for monitor ad businesses is complete.
insights.quote: the privacy policies for monitors by companies LG, Samsung, and Acer (Acer also makes smart monitors) all state that the companies may share data collected from its devices with advertisers
insights.locator: For the record, the privacy policies

insights.claim: A smart monitor exposes the user to three tracking layers simultaneously — the display maker, the OS operator such as Google for Android-powered models, and third-party app providers such as Netflix — each with its own lengthy policy.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Stacked data collection makes consumer consent effectively unattainable, which is the structural argument regulators eventually act on.

themes.theme: The TV playbook as forward-looking template

insights.claim: Smart TVs also had a logical, consumer-friendly purpose before the industry started pumping them with ads, which is the author's basis for expecting smart monitors to follow the same trajectory despite genuine current demand.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The reusable pattern: connected hardware categories start useful and monetize later — assume ad-subsidy capture in any newly connected device class.
insights.quote: But smart TVs also had a logical, consumer-friendly purpose before the industry started pumping them with ads.
insights.locator: There are reasons for smart monitors to exist

insights.claim: Ads and operating systems could one day drive down monitor prices as they did TV prices, but the author would rather see manufacturers compete on new display technology, improved audio, or other capabilities.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: If ad subsidy takes hold, monitor hardware margins compress toward the TV model and recurring ad revenue becomes the real business line.
insights.locator: Ads and OSes could one day help drive down

insights.claim: The author's worst case is that dumb monitors become as rare as dumb TVs, and argues regular monitors should remain widely available as they are now.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Availability of non-connected displays is the tail risk for privacy-sensitive buyers and a potential niche for a differentiated vendor.
insights.quote: It would be outrageous if dumb monitors were one day as rare as dumb TVs.
insights.locator: Regular monitors should also remain widely available

insights.claim: Most smart monitors do allow users to disable tracking, but the settings must be dug out of menus rather than being presented during setup — the author cites Apple TV as hardware that makes privacy policies easy to understand and tracking easy to disable at plug-in.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Default-on tracking with buried opt-outs is the industry norm; Apple's setup-time disclosure is the differentiator competitors could copy but choose not to.
insights.quote: Apple TV is a great example of hardware that makes it easy to understand privacy policies and to disable tracking settings right when you plug it in.
insights.locator: And with smart monitors being a newer product
